subject: physics
title: Development of the atomic model
key_idea: Scientists change a model when new evidence cannot be explained by the old one. The plum pudding model was replaced by the nuclear model after the alpha particle scattering experiment. Bohr then added electrons orbiting at set distances.

blocks.text: A scientific model is an idea that explains the evidence. This section covers why models are changed or replaced.

items: New experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced.
A model is replaced when it cannot explain the new evidence, or when its predictions are shown to be incorrect.
The new model must explain the new evidence, and its predictions must be shown to be correct.
The atom is an example. Our ideas about it have changed as experiments, equipment, collaboration between scientists and peer review improved.
New evidence that the old model cannot explain leads to a new model.
The new model must explain the new evidence.

sections.heading: From the plum pudding model to the nuclear model

blocks.text: Before the electron was discovered, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided. The discovery of the electron changed this.

items.meaning: The atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it (Thomson).
The mass of the atom is concentrated at the centre in a charged nucleus, with electrons around it.
An experiment in which alpha particles are fired at thin gold foil and the angles they scatter through are detected (Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden).

Nuclear model

blocks.text: The alpha particle scattering results did not fit the plum pudding model. Each observation points to a conclusion about the atom.

rows: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
The atom has a charged nucleus that repels alpha particles.
Very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles, a few bouncing straight back.
The nucleus is small, dense and positively charged.

items: The plum pudding model did not predict that some particles would be deflected.
The large angle deflections show that the atom contains a nucleus.
All the deflections show that the nucleus is charged.
The nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
The plum pudding model has positive charge spread out, with electrons embedded in it.
Scattering results showed a small, charged nucleus that holds the mass, with mostly empty space around it.

blocks.text: The nuclear model was then improved in several steps.

items: Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
Bohr's theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.
Later experiments showed that the positive charge of a nucleus can be divided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same positive charge. These particles were named protons.
James Chadwick's experimental work provided the evidence for neutrons in the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted idea.

diagram.prompt: Put these ideas about the atom in the order they were developed.
steps: Atoms are tiny spheres that cannot be divided
The electron is discovered, giving the plum pudding model
Alpha scattering leads to the nuclear model
Bohr suggests electrons orbit at specific distances
Protons are named as the particles of positive charge
Chadwick provides the evidence for neutrons

items: Bohr added electrons orbiting the nucleus at specific distances.
Protons were named from the charge of the nucleus, and Chadwick showed that neutrons exist.

checks.q: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
checks.a: The atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

checks.q: Most alpha particles passed straight through gold foil, but a few were deflected through large angles. State two conclusions.
checks.a: Most of the atom is empty space. The atom has a small, charged nucleus that holds the mass.

checks.q: Explain why scientists replace an old model with a new one.
checks.a: New evidence cannot be explained by the old model, or its predictions are shown to be incorrect. The new model explains the new evidence.

worked_example.question:
Sometimes an old scientific model is replaced by a new model.

Explain why scientists replace an old scientific model with a new model. Include an example from Physics in your answer.
answer_points: There is new experimental evidence or data.
The evidence cannot be explained using the existing model, or predictions made using the old model are shown to be incorrect.
The new model explains the new evidence, or its predictions are shown to be correct.
A suitable example, for example the nuclear model of the atom replacing the plum pudding model.
worked_example.tip: One mark each. Other examples are accepted, such as the heliocentric model replacing the geocentric model.

worked_example.question: Explain how the difference in the number of particles scattered at different angles gives evidence for the current model of the structure of the atom.
answer_points: Most alpha particles pass straight through the foil with little deflection.
Some alpha particles are scattered through small angles, less than 90 degrees.
Very few alpha particles are scattered through large angles, greater than 90 degrees.
Atoms are mainly empty space, and there must be a nucleus that is small, heavy or dense, and charged.
worked_example.tip: Any four points from the observations and conclusions score. A back-scattered particle can be described as rebounding or bouncing back.

worked_example.question:
The atomic model has changed over time. Three scientists who contributed to the atomic model are Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr.

One of these three scientists did an experiment where alpha particles were fired at a thin piece of gold foil. Two important observations were recorded.

What did the scientist conclude about the atom from these observations?

Observation 1: Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil.
Observation 2: Some of the alpha particles were deflected.
answer_points: Observation 1: most of the atom is empty space.
Observation 2: the atom has a positively charged nucleus.
worked_example.tip: One mark for empty space, one for positively charged and one for nucleus. A very small nucleus is also allowed.

worked_example.question:
An experiment directs alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold foil. Some of the alpha particles are deflected through angles less than 90° and a few are deflected through 180°.

State and explain two conclusions about the nuclei of atoms from this observation.
answer_points: The nucleus is very small, because not many alpha particles pass close to the nucleus.
The mass of the gold nucleus is much greater than the mass of an alpha particle, because the large force from the nucleus has a bigger effect on the small mass of the alpha particle.
The nucleus is positively charged, because alpha particles are positively charged and the force on them is repulsive.
Any two conclusions, each with its matching explanation, score the 4 marks.

blocks.text: The scattering of alpha particles by thin metal foil gives evidence for three things about the nucleus.

items: It is very small, with the atom mostly empty space: most alpha particles pass straight through and very few are deflected through large angles.
It contains most of the mass of the atom: an alpha particle bounces back only from something much heavier than itself.
It is positively charged: the positive alpha particles are repelled as they pass close to it.
